introduction: A container image is a packaged process. Kubernetes adds an API and controllers that keep a declared number of those processes running. In this lesson, you will watch a deleted process return because its desired state still exists.

Use Taskboard's already-tested stage03 in-memory adapter to isolate orchestration from database administration. Its data disappears when a Pod is replaced and differs between replicas. That is a deliberate platform exercise, not a deployable multi-user storage design. The cluster lives in Docker on one computer; two Pods do not create two-machine availability.
prerequisites: Ubuntu 24.04 Bash in WSL2 or a disposable Linux VM; Docker is running. Use the same terminal unless a step names a second terminal.

Completed Docker and testing lessons; supplied Taskboard copied to ~/dev-opps-lab/app/taskboard. curl, Python 3, tar and Docker CLI available; allow several GB of local image space. No public ports or paid resources are created.

concepts.title: One request, several responsibilities
paragraphs: kubectl sends your object to the API server. The server authenticates and authorizes the request and stores desired state in etcd. A Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which owns Pods. A scheduler assigns a pending Pod to a suitable node. The node's kubelet asks its container runtime to run the image.
Each component observes and retries. An accepted manifest does not mean the image exists, a node has capacity, or an HTTP request succeeds.
concepts.example: A Deployment asks for two replicas; deleting one Pod changes observed state, so the ReplicaSet requests a replacement.
concepts.judgment: Observe the failed boundary before changing everything. A missing image is a registry/runtime problem, not evidence that the scheduler is broken.

concepts.title: Declarative ownership
paragraphs: A manifest describes desired fields. Controllers reconcile those fields after failures. The Deployment owns the Pod template; changing an individual Pod cannot reliably change future replicas.

The podinfo learning repository supplies a known workload for isolating platform faults. We use the same principle with familiar stage03 code: keep business behavior simple while learning object ownership.
concepts.example: ReplicaSet names and Pod UIDs change; the Deployment name and intended image remain stable.
concepts.judgment: Reconciliation proves declared mechanics, not business correctness. Kubernetes cannot infer that a task belongs to the wrong person.

steps.title: Install clients and create an isolated cluster
steps.purpose: Use a separate kubeconfig so commands cannot silently target another cluster.

commands.code:
mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" "$HOME/dev-opps-lab/k8s" "$HOME/dev-opps-lab/evidence/w25"
cd "$HOME/dev-opps-lab/k8s"
case "$(uname -m)" in x86_64) ARCH=amd64 ;; aarch64) ARCH=arm64 ;; *) echo 'Unsupported CPU'; exit 1 ;; esac
curl -fL "https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/dl/v0.33.0/kind-linux-$ARCH" -o "$HOME/.local/bin/kind"
KUBECTL_VERSION=$(curl -fsSL https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)
curl -fL "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$KUBECTL_VERSION/bin/linux/$ARCH/kubectl" -o kubectl
curl -fL "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$KUBECTL_VERSION/bin/linux/$ARCH/kubectl.sha256" -o kubectl.sha256
printf '%s  kubectl
' "$(cat kubectl.sha256)" | sha256sum --check
install -m 0755 kubectl "$HOME/.local/bin/kubectl"
chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/kind"
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
export KUBECONFIG="$HOME/dev-opps-lab/k8s/kubeconfig"
kind create cluster --name devopps --kubeconfig "$KUBECONFIG" --wait 120s
kubectl config current-context
kubectl version
kind version
explain: mkdir -p creates reusable directories; cd makes all following manifest paths explicit. uname reports CPU architecture; case chooses the matching release binary or exits.

curl -f fails on HTTP errors, -L follows official redirects, -sS keeps failures visible while suppressing progress. stable.txt is resolved once into KUBECTL_VERSION; record it rather than assuming a future latest release behaves identically.

printf supplies the checksum file name; the pipe passes it to sha256sum --check. Stop on a FAILED checksum. install -m 0755 copies the client with executable permissions; chmod does the same for kind. PATH affects this terminal.

KUBECONFIG points to this lab's file. kind --name scopes its Docker resources; --wait waits for a ready API. current-context must be kind-devopps. kubectl version reports client/server versions; keep the client within one minor version of the server.
commands.expected: Context kind-devopps; a Kubernetes server version and kind v0.33.0.
commands.troubleshoot: If Docker cannot be reached, fix docker info first. A version-skew warning requires a matching kubectl release, not suppressing the warning. On a repeat run inspect kind get clusters instead of overwriting unrelated configuration.

steps.checkpoint: Save the two tool versions and the node image from docker inspect devopps-control-plane.

steps.title: Deploy a known image
steps.purpose: Build once and load that local artifact into kind.

commands.code:
cd "$HOME/dev-opps-lab/app/taskboard"
docker build --target runtime -t devopps-taskboard:w25 .
kind load docker-image devopps-taskboard:w25 --name devopps
kubectl create namespace devopps
cd "$HOME/dev-opps-lab/k8s"
cat > app.yaml <<'YAML'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: taskboard
  namespace: devopps
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: taskboard}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: taskboard}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: devopps-taskboard:w25
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        command: [python, -m, uvicorn, 'reference.stage03:app', --host, 0.0.0.0, --port, '8000', --no-access-log]
        ports:
        - {name: http, containerPort: 8000}
        resources:
          requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 96Mi}
          limits: {memory: 192Mi}
YAML
kubectl apply -f app.yaml
kubectl -n devopps rollout status deployment/taskboard --timeout=120s
kubectl -n devopps get deployment,replicaset,pods -o wide
explain: docker build uses the supplied Dockerfile runtime target; -t gives this immutable-for-the-exercise build a distinct local tag. kind load imports it into the node runtime; your laptop Docker image store is not automatically the node store.

create namespace isolates names. The quoted YAML heredoc writes literal configuration. replicas is the target count; selector must match template labels. IfNotPresent permits the preloaded image. The command deliberately selects the stage03 adapter on port8000.

100m means one tenth of a CPU request. 96Mi is the scheduling memory request; 192Mi is the memory ceiling. apply submits the document; rollout status waits for its replicas; get -o wide adds node/IP observations.
commands.expected: Two Ready Pods belonging to one ReplicaSet; Deployment READY 2/2.
commands.troubleshoot: Use kubectl -n devopps describe pod POD_NAME with a name from get pods. FailedScheduling points to capacity; image events point to image retrieval. Do not blindly increase permissions.

steps.checkpoint: Identify the Deployment→ReplicaSet→Pod chain before the next step.

steps.title: Observe replacement
steps.purpose: Compare object identity before and after deleting one disposable replica.

commands.code:
POD=$(kubectl -n devopps get pods -l app=taskboard -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n devopps get pod "$POD" -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}{"
"}{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}{"
"}'
kubectl -n devopps delete pod "$POD"
kubectl -n devopps rollout status deployment/taskboard --timeout=120s
kubectl -n devopps get pods -l app=taskboard -o wide
kubectl -n devopps logs deployment/taskboard --tail=20
explain: $(...) stores one selected Pod name. -l filters by the label, and jsonpath selects name, UID and owner fields without copying a changing name by hand.
delete removes that one Pod, not its controller. rollout status waits for replacement. logs deployment selects a Pod for application stdout; --tail=20 bounds the output.
commands.expected: A different Pod name/UID appears and desired replicas remain two.
commands.troubleshoot: If it does not return, inspect ReplicaSet desired/current counts and namespace events. Application logs alone cannot explain why a Pod was never scheduled.

steps.checkpoint: Write five sentences, one per control-plane/runtime responsibility.

failure.title: The declared image does not exist
failure.boundary: Only the taskboard Deployment in the disposable devopps namespace. Read recovery first.

explain: set image changes the controller template and begins a new rollout.
inject.expected: A new Pod cannot start; an old Ready replica may remain.
inject.troubleshoot: Inspect events; do not delete healthy old replicas.

investigate.code:
kubectl -n devopps get pods
kubectl -n devopps get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
explain: get pods locates the affected replica. Sorting events by creationTimestamp puts recent image failures last.
investigate.expected: ErrImagePull followed by ImagePullBackOff or a registry authorization failure for the nonexistent tag.
investigate.troubleshoot: A private-registry authentication error and a missing tag are different hypotheses; read the event message.

hints: Does the existing good image still exist in the kind node?

explanation: The scheduler assigned work, but the kubelet/runtime could not obtain the requested artifact. Backoff reduces repeated retries; restarting the controller cannot make the tag exist.

explain: Reapply the recorded good source manifest.
recover.troubleshoot: Compare the live image to app.yaml if a rollout still fails.

verification.code:
kubectl -n devopps rollout status deployment/taskboard --timeout=120s
kubectl -n devopps get deployment taskboard -o jsonpath="{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}"
explain: Wait for recovery, then print the effective image.
verification.troubleshoot: Inspect the newest events rather than old failure events.

questions.prompt: Why does deleting a Pod not reduce desired capacity?
questions.answer: The ReplicaSet still desires two Pods; the Deployment still desires that ReplicaSet template. Change the owner to intentionally scale.

questions.prompt: Why can a loaded image still be pulled from a registry?
questions.answer: Always initiates registry resolution. An exact preloaded tag with IfNotPresent avoids it in this local exercise; production promotion should use an immutable digest.

questions.hint: Think about an HTTP request and its data.
questions.answer: It describes process state, not readiness, correct authorization, durable storage or a user action. Those need separate evidence.

exercise.brief: Scale the declared Deployment to three replicas and prove replacement without editing a Pod.
constraints: Change app.yaml first; keep the stage03 data limitation explicit.
acceptance: One deleted Pod replaced with a new UID
solution: Set replicas:3 in app.yaml, apply it, observe the ReplicaSet, and delete one selected Pod. Restore replicas:2 for the next lesson.

explain: Return live capacity to two. Keep app.yaml at two also; retain this named local cluster for week26.
cleanup.troubleshoot: If ending the level now, kind delete cluster --name devopps removes only this disposable cluster; retain manifests/evidence to rebuild.

references.title: kind quick start
references.usedFor: Pinned installer, kubeconfig and local image loading

repoConnections.principle: Use a known workload to separate platform faults from business faults.
repoConnections.application: The same reasoning will let you compare a failing Taskboard Pod with a working reference workload, rather than treating every incident as a cluster failure.

notes: Commands are authored and documentation-checked; this authoring host has no Docker/Kubernetes runtime, so cluster execution is not claimed.
title: Learn reconciliation on a local cluster
outcome: Explain what the API server, scheduler, controllers, kubelet and container runtime do.
